c

items.situation: You are four minutes early on a call with one American. Say something.
tips: The only wrong answer is silence.

items.situation: Ask a stranger how long they have been with the company, softly.
tips: Could you tell me how long you have been with the company?
Statement order inside. Not how long have you been.

items.situation: You want to know if their team is on the monthly call. Ask.
tips: Do you know whether your team is on the monthly call?

items.situation: Confirm that this is the person who wrote the report, and hand the turn back.
tips: You are the one who wrote the report, aren't you?
The tag is what keeps the conversation alive.

items.situation: Ask for twenty minutes of somebody time while you are there.
tips: I was wondering if you would have twenty minutes while I am here.
Leave them a way to say no. It is what makes yes easy.

items.situation: They said we should grab lunch sometime. Turn it into a plan.
tips: Would Thursday work, or is Friday easier for you?
Name a day. Sometime is a friendly noise.

listenings.text: People from outside the US think small talk is a waste of four minutes. It is not four minutes of nothing, it is four minutes of finding out how to talk to you. In that time I am working out how direct I can be with you, whether you want to be asked about your family, whether you are the kind of person who answers a question with a joke, and roughly how senior you feel. All of that changes how I run the next fifty minutes. So if you skip it, I do not think you are efficient. I think I have no idea who I am talking to, and I get more careful, not less. The other thing to know is that nobody expects the answer to be interesting. How was your weekend is not a request for information. It is a handshake with words, and the only wrong answer is silence.

Three things, and I got all of them wrong for about a year. The first is that I answered questions completely. Somebody asked how the project was going and I gave them four minutes. They wanted twenty seconds and a door to walk through. The second is that I waited to be invited. In Brazil somebody senior brings you in. Here, if you want twenty minutes with the plant director, you ask the plant director, and nobody thinks it is strange. I lost most of a year waiting for an introduction that was never coming. And the third one still catches me. When an American says we should grab lunch sometime, that is not a plan, it is a friendly noise. If you want the lunch, you have to say which day. Say Thursday. They will say yes or they will say Friday. Either way you have a lunch, which is more than I had in my first year.
